paragraphs: Alyosha went to his father first. On the way he remembered that his father had insisted the day before that he must come without his brother Ivan seeing him. “Why?” Alyosha suddenly wondered. “Even if Father has something to say to me alone, why should I go in unseen? Most likely he meant to say something else yesterday, he was so worked up,” he decided. Still, he was very glad when Marfa Ignatyevna opened the garden gate for him (Grigory, it turned out, was ill in bed in the lodge) and, in answer to his question, told him that Ivan Fyodorovitch had gone out two hours earlier.
“And my father?”
“He’s up, having his coffee,” Marfa answered, a little curtly.

Alyosha went in. The old man was sitting alone at the table in slippers and a shabby little overcoat. He was passing the time looking over some accounts, though without much attention. He was entirely alone in the house, since Smerdyakov had gone out to the market too. He had risen early and was trying to put a bold face on things, but he looked tired and weak. A red handkerchief was bound round his forehead, where huge purple bruises had come out overnight. His nose had swollen terribly in the night as well, and smaller bruises were spread over it in patches. All this gave his face a peculiarly spiteful, irritable look. The old man knew it, and as Alyosha came in he gave him a hostile glare.
“The coffee’s gone cold,” he cried harshly. “I won’t offer you any. Today I’ve ordered nothing but a Lenten fish soup, and I’m not asking anyone to share it. Why are you here?”
“To see how you are,” said Alyosha.
“Yes. And I did tell you to come yesterday. It’s of no importance. You needn’t have gone to the trouble. But I knew you’d come poking your nose in right away.”

He said this with something close to hostility. At the same moment he got up and anxiously checked his nose in the looking-glass (perhaps for the fortieth time that morning). He also started tying the red handkerchief round his forehead more becomingly.
“Red is better. A white one makes me look like I’m in the hospital,” he pronounced gravely. “Well, how are things over there? How’s your elder?”
“He is very ill. He may die today,” Alyosha answered. But his father hadn’t listened, and had forgotten his own question at once.

“Ivan’s gone out,” he said suddenly. “He’s trying his hardest to take Mitya’s betrothed away from him. That’s what he’s staying here for,” he added spitefully, and gave Alyosha a sidelong look with his mouth twisted.
“Surely he never told you that?” asked Alyosha.
“He did, a long time ago. Believe it or not, he told me three weeks back. You don’t imagine he came here to murder me as well, do you? He must have come for some reason.”
“What do you mean? Why do you say such things?” said Alyosha, upset.

“He doesn’t ask for money, it’s true, but he’ll not get a farthing out of me all the same. I mean to live as long as I can, you may as well know, my dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, and so I need every farthing, and the longer I live, the more I’ll need,” he went on, pacing from one corner of the room to the other, his hands in the pockets of his loose, greasy overcoat of yellow cotton. “I can still pass for a man of fifty-five, but I want to go on passing for one another twenty years. The older I get, you know, the less pretty I’ll be. The wenches won’t come to me for nothing, so I’ll need my money. That’s why I’m saving up more and more, just for myself, my dear son Alexey Fyodorovitch. You may as well know that. Because I mean to go on sinning to the end, let me tell you. Sin is sweet. Everybody curses it, and everybody lives in it, only the others do it on the sly and I do it in the open. And that’s why all the other sinners jump on me, for being so simple. And your paradise, Alexey Fyodorovitch, isn’t to my taste, let me tell you. It’s no place for a gentleman, your paradise, even if there is such a thing. I believe I fall asleep and never wake up, and that’s the end of it. Pray for my soul if you like. If you don’t want to, then don’t, damn you! That’s my philosophy. Ivan spoke well here yesterday, though we were all drunk. Ivan is a conceited coxcomb, but he has no great learning ... no education either. He sits there silent, smiling at you and saying nothing—that’s what gets him by.”
Alyosha listened to him in silence.

“Why won’t he talk to me? When he does speak, he puts on airs. Your Ivan is a scoundrel! And if I want to, I’ll marry Grushenka in a minute. If you’ve got money, Alexey Fyodorovitch, you only have to want something and you can have it. That’s what Ivan is afraid of. He’s watching to stop me from marrying, and that’s why he’s egging Mitya on to marry Grushenka himself. He hopes that will keep me away from Grushenka (as if I’d leave him my money if I don’t marry her!). And if Mitya marries Grushenka, Ivan can carry off his rich betrothed. That’s what he’s counting on! He’s a scoundrel, your Ivan!”
“How cross you are! It’s from yesterday. You had better lie down,” said Alyosha.

“There! You say that,” the old man remarked suddenly, as if it had only now occurred to him, “and I’m not angry with you. If Ivan said it, I’d be angry with him. It’s only with you that I have my good moments. Otherwise, you know, I’m an ill-natured man.”
“You’re not ill-natured. You’re warped,” said Alyosha, smiling.

“Listen. This morning I meant to have that ruffian Mitya locked up, and now I don’t know what I’ll decide. Of course, nowadays, with all this fashion, fathers and mothers count as a prejudice. But even now the law doesn’t let a son drag his old father around by the hair, kick him in the face in his own house, and boast that he’ll murder him outright—and all of it with witnesses present. If I wanted, I could crush him and have him locked up straight away for what he did yesterday.”
“Then you don’t intend to bring charges?”
“Ivan talked me out of it. I wouldn’t care what Ivan thinks, but there’s something else.”
And bending toward Alyosha, he went on in a confidential half-whisper.

“If I put the ruffian in prison, she’ll hear of it and run to see him at once. But if she hears that he beat me, a weak old man, to within an inch of my life, she might give him up and come to me.... That’s how she is, everything by contraries. I know her through and through! Won’t you have a drop of brandy? Have some cold coffee and I’ll pour a quarter of a glass of brandy into it. It’s delicious, my boy.”

“No, thank you. I’ll take that roll along, if I may,” said Alyosha. He took a halfpenny French roll and put it in the pocket of his cassock. “And you shouldn’t have brandy either,” he suggested nervously, looking into the old man’s face.
“You’re right, it only upsets my nerves instead of calming them. Just one little glass. I’ll get it out of the cupboard.”
He unlocked the cupboard, poured a glass and drank it, then locked the cupboard again and put the key back in his pocket.
“That’s enough. One glass won’t kill me.”
“You see, you’re in a better mood now,” said Alyosha with a smile.

“Hm! I love you even without the brandy, but with scoundrels I’m a scoundrel. Ivan’s not going to Tchermashnya—why is that? He wants to spy and find out how much I give Grushenka if she comes. They’re all scoundrels! I don’t recognize Ivan, I don’t know him at all. Where does he come from? He’s not one of us in his soul. As if I’d leave him anything! I won’t leave a will at all, you may as well know. And I’ll crush Mitya like a beetle. I squash black-beetles at night with my slipper, they squelch when you step on them. And your Mitya will squelch too. _Your_ Mitya, because you love him. Yes, you love him, and I’m not afraid of you loving him. But if Ivan loved him, I’d be afraid, for myself, of his loving him. But Ivan loves nobody. Ivan is not one of us. People like Ivan aren’t our kind, my boy. They’re like a cloud of dust. The wind blows, and the dust is gone.... I had a silly idea in my head when I told you to come today. I wanted to find out from you about Mitya. Suppose I handed him a thousand now, or maybe two. Would the beggarly wretch agree to clear off altogether for five years or, better still, thirty-five, and without Grushenka, and give her up once and for all, eh?”
“I—I’ll ask him,” Alyosha muttered. “If you would give him three thousand, perhaps he—”

“That’s nonsense! No need to ask him now, no need! I’ve changed my mind. It was a nonsensical idea. I’ll give him nothing, not a penny, I want my money for myself,” cried the old man, waving his hand. “I’ll crush him like a beetle without it. Don’t say a word to him, or he’ll start hoping. There’s nothing for you to do here, you needn’t stay. That betrothed of his, Katerina Ivanovna, whom he’s kept so carefully hidden from me all this time, is she going to marry him or not? You went to see her yesterday, I believe?”
“Nothing will make her give him up.”

“There, you see how dearly these fine young ladies love a rake and a scoundrel. They’re poor creatures, I tell you, those pale young ladies, very different from—Ah, if I had his youth and the looks I had then (because at twenty-eight I was better-looking than he is), I’d have been a conquering hero just as he is. He’s a low cad! But he won’t have Grushenka, anyway, he won’t! I’ll crush him!”
His anger had flared up again with those last words.
“Go on, you can go. There’s nothing for you to do here today,” he snapped harshly.
Alyosha went up to say good-by to him, and kissed him on the shoulder.
“What’s that for?” The old man was a little surprised. “We’ll see each other again, or do you think we won’t?”
“Not at all, I didn’t mean anything.”

“Neither did I, I didn’t mean anything,” said the old man, looking at him. “Listen, listen,” he shouted after him, “come back soon and I’ll have a fish soup for you, a fine one, not like today’s. Be sure to come! Come tomorrow, do you hear, tomorrow!”
And as soon as Alyosha had gone out of the door, he went to the cupboard again and poured another half-glass.

“I won’t have any more!” he muttered, clearing his throat. Again he locked the cupboard and put the key in his pocket. Then he went into his bedroom and lay down on the bed, worn out, and in a minute he was asleep.
